AB Roy Chowdhury------For the Petitioners. 
Carib Newaz with Maksuda Aktar------For Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Abdus Sukur (Md) and others  ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Bhasani Mandal and another  ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
This Rule was obtained by the plaintiffs upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgment and decree dated 9-5-2000 passed by Additional District Judge, 3rd Court at Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 748 of 1999 reversing those dated  30-9-1999 passed by Senior Assistant Judge, 6th Court at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 249 of 1998.

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs on 28-7-1998 instituted the suit for setting aside the judgment and decree dated 24-5-1998 and 31-5-1998 respectively, exhibit 12 and 12 (ka) obtained by defendant No.1 from 3rd Court of Additional Assistant Judge at *Civil Revision No. 3535 of 2000 Dhaka in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 and also for declaration that those are not operative against and binding upon the plaintiffs.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that after successive transactions, the suit land measuring about 96 decimals of CS and SA Plot No. 1244 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 212 and SA Khatian No. 507 were owned and possessed by defendant No. 1 and his brother Sudhir Mandai. Then, both of them transferred the suit land to Parul Bal by a registered deed of sale dated 14-5-1969 being deed No. 4400, exhibit 4 and delivered possession. Then, on 4-2-1970 Parul Balal transferred the suit land to one Sufia Khatun by a registered deed of sale being deed No. 1126, exhibit 5 and delivered possession. Sufia Khatun got her name mutated and possessed the suit land for quite some time on payment of rents and then, on 9-12-1977 she transferred by a registered kabala being deed No. 35842, exhibit 7 to Sahabuddin and delivered possession. Then, by about 30 sale deeds exhibit 9 series, Sahabuddin transferred the suit land to the plaintiffs from 1979 to 1984 and delivered possession. The plaintiffs after purchase got their names mutated in respect of their respective land and now, possess the same in their specific share by raising dwelling huts, etc. and on payment of rents.

4. On 8-7-1998 the plaintiffs got a notice issued by the local Demra Police Station on the basis of a complaint dated 7-7-1998 lodged by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, and therefrom, they came to learn for the first time that the defendants claimed to have obtained the aforesaid judgment and decree in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997. Obtaining a certified copy of the same, they found that the defendants got the deed of sale to Parul Bala dated 14-5-1969 exhibit 4 cancelled in the said judgment and decree.

5. Defendant No. 1 alone contested the suit by filing a written statement. His case, in brief, is that he and his brother acquired the entire suit land of 96 decimals. The suit land is nal land i.e. agricultural land. He possesses half 48 decimals of land through borgadar, till today. His brother Sudhir died issueless and his wife got the other half in limited interest. And now Parul Bala lives in her said half. On 8-8-1995 he heard from Zinnah and others that he and his brother sold their land to Parol Bala in 1969. Then, he obtained certified copies of the deeds of the land and became sure about the transfer. Then, he instituted Title Suit No.180 of 1995 which was on transfer renumbered as Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 and got the judgment and decree dated 24-5-1998 and 31- 5-1998 on contest against Parol Bala.

6. On the pleadings, 3 issues were raised. Of them, issue No. 1 is whether the suit as framed is maintainable or not and issue No.2 is whether the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 are liable to be set aside as void and not binding upon the plaintiffs or not. Plaintiffs examined 6 witnesses while defendant No. 1 examined 2 witnesses including himself. Plaintiffs' documents were marked as exhibits 1 to 12 series while those of the defendant No. 1 exhibit No. 'Ka' to 'Ja'. But Parul Bala did neither contest the suit nor appeared as a witness.

7. The trial Court decreed the suit as prayed for. On appeal by said defendant No. 1, the Court of appeal below allowed the appeal and set side the judgment, and decree of the trial Court by the impugned judgment and decree.

<u>8. Mr AB Roy Chowdhury, learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that all the documents of the plaintiffs were duly admitted without any objection and proved, but the Court of appeal below without seeing the documents on record held that the execution of those documents were not proved and thus, it erred in law in dismissing the suit upon such erroneous view which has resulted in failure of justice. He then submits that the Court of appeal below without reversing the findings of the trial Court and adverting to the reasons given, erred in law in setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court. He also submits that the Court of appeal below also erred in law in considering certain things which are not at all necessary for disposal of the appeal. He cites the decision in the case of Haider Ali vs the State, 47 DLR (AD) 46 and that of Moulavi Abdul Mannan vs Md Rafiqul Islam, 46 DLR 493.</u>

<u>9. Mr Garib Newaz, learned Advocate for opposite party No.1 (defendant No.1) submits that the suit as framed is not maintainable under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for want of further declaration of title in the suit land. He then submits that by judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997, the sale deed dated 14- 5-1969, exhibit 4 was cancelled to the extent of half share of the defendant No. 1 only and the appellate. Court having upheld such cancellation committed no error calling for any interference. He also submits that the finding of the appellate Court that the plaintiffs have no possession in the suit land on consideration of the evidence on record and such finding being a finding on fact must be held to have been concluded by the decision of the final Court of facts. He also supports the view of the Court of appeal below that the plaint was not signed by many of the plaintiffs. He cites, on admission and execution of documents, the decision in the case of Jhanda Singh and another vs Harman Singh and others, AIR 1926 Lahore 415, Sheikh Karimullah vs Gudar Koeri and others, AIR 1925 Allahabad 56 and Gopal Das and another vs Sri Thakurji and others, AIR 1936 Allahabad 422.</u>

10. In reply, Mr Roy Chowdhury submits that the finding of the Court of appeal below on possession is based on misreading and non-reading of the evidence oral and documentary on record. So such finding is not binding in revision. He further submits that all the title deeds of the plaintiffs exhibits 13 series were admitted by the executant thereof, PW 4 Sahabuddin. He also took me through the judgment of the trial Court again and showed the findings on which the trial Court held the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 collusive and fraudulent which were not at all considered by the Court of appeal below.

11. It appears from the record that by judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997, exhibit No. 12 and 12 (ka) the sale deed being No. 4400 dated 14-5-1969, exhibit No.4 executed by defendant No. 1 and his brother Sudhir Mandai in favour of Parul Bala was declared to be forged, false, fraudulent and collusive, and thereby, the title of defendant No. 1 in 48 decimals of land as described in schedule 'Kha' to the plaint of the previous suit was not affected. In the trial of the suit, issue No.2, as stated earlier, is whether the above judgment and decree, exhibit No. 12 and 12 (ka) as obtained by defendant No. 1 in his Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 are liable to be set aside as void, and also not binding upon the plaintiffs or not? On finding of various facts and circumstances, the trial Court held that by impleading only Parul Bala and without making the plaintiffs parties in the suit, defendant No. 1 obtained said judgment and decree in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 through collusion and by practicing fraud. Court of appeal below also formulated issue No. 1 as' whether the decree passed in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 was obtained illegally and fraudulently and, as such, liable to be set aside. This is the moot issue in the suit.

12. On the issue, the case of the plaintiffs' in short, is that divested of all their right, title, interest or possession in the suit land about 30 years ago, defendant No.1, Bhasani Mandai and No.2, Parul Bala went to India and settled there permanently. Now, they got the suit instituted and obtained impugned judgment and decree through false personification, and also by collusion with each other and practicing fraud upon the Court. The case of the defendant No.1 is that he has long been living in Bangladesh, possesses the suit land by cultivation through borgadar and Parul Bala lives in her other half of the suit land in three huts. He is now living at 66/A Dinanath Sen Road. But exhibit No. 11, a notice dated 8-7-1998 issued by Demra PS on the complaint dated 7-7-1998 as lodged by defendant No.1, and No.2, Parul Bala shows that they are both living at the time in the same address of Dinanath Sen Road.

13. Let me first see the findings of the appellate Court. It appears that the appeal was allowed on the findings to the effect that from the evidence of the PWs, it appeared to it that they do not have any idea of the suit land and the plaintiffs have no possession; that by the sale deed dated 14-5-1969 exhibit No.4 no title of Parul Bala was established; that by sale deeds, exhibit Nos. 5, 7 and 8 no title was transferred to the subsequent purchasers and they did not acquire any title; and that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title in the suit land and their deeds (exhibit 9 series, numbering 30) are nothing but papers.

14. In the next breath, the appellate Court however held that by the impugned sale deed (exhibit 4) the title of the defendant No. 1 would not be affected. Said sale deed would only be applicable to the share of Parul Bala, successor to Sudhir MandaI. Therefore, the judgment delivered in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 dated 24-5-1998 is valid and in accordance with law.

15. As stated earlier, by said judgment and decree passed in the previous suit the sale deed dated 14-5-1969 exhibit No.4 was cancelled as collusive and forged. The Court of appeal below wants us to accept the said judgment as half invalid in respect of the share of defendant No. 1 only but valid in respect of other half, i.e. in respect of Parul Bala. According to the appellate Court, the trial Court therefore committed mistake in decreeing the suit. But the appellate Court dismissed the suit in its entirety. This view of the appellate Court is preposterous on the face of it.

16. I will now see why the decree dated 12 (ka) as impugned in the instant suit was set aside by the trial Court. On elaborate consideration of the evidence on record, the trial. Court found that defendant No.2 Parul Bala contested the earlier suit by filing a written statement denying the case of the defendant No. 1 but during cross-examination she admitted entire case of defendant No. 1 saying that defendant No. 1 and her husband Sudhir did not execute the sale deed exhibit No.4 dated 14-5-1969. Parul Bala was though living with defendant No. 1 in the same address of Dinanath Sen Road but she did neither contest the instant suit nor appear before the Court to support the defendant No. 1 as before. The predecessors of the plaintiffs possessed the suit land and now, the plaintiffs possess on raising dwellings. Defendant No.1 failed to prove that he had been in Bangladesh from 1970 to 1995. Title documents of the plaintiffs were admitted by the executant Sahabuddin to have been executed by him as PW 4 and that defendant No. 1 obtained the judgment and decree in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 without impleading the plaintiffs. In coming to such findings various reasons were also given by the trial Court.

17. But the above facts and circumstances as weighed with the trial Court did not find any favour of the Court of appeal below. It appears from the plaint of earlier Title Suit No. 51 of 1997. Parol Bala was made defendant No. 1 and the Sub-Registrar, Mohammadpur, Registration Complex, Tejgaon, Dhaka was made defendant No.2. Address of both the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were given same of Dogar, Demra, Parul Bala appeared in the suit and filed a written statement contending that defendant No. 1 and his brother executed sale deed dated 14-5-1969 in her favour. Having learnt that the original deed was not in her custody, defendant No. 1 now denied the execution. But during the cross-examination she as DW-1 made a u-turn and stated that her husband and defendant No. 1 never gave her any deed. She enjoyed the share of her husband. She did not' claim the share of Bhasani Mandai, defendant No. 1. She could not say how a deed of sale came into existence. It is on record that after purchase from Parul Bala by sale deed, exhibit No. 5 Sufia Khatun got her name mutated and she possessed the suit land for some time on payment of rents and RS record of rights was also prepared in her name. Then, Sahabuddin possessed the suit land till he sold to the plaintiffs from 1979 to 1984. The notice dated 8-7-1998 exhibit No. 11 issued by Demra Police upon a complaint dated 7-7-1998 lodged by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 informing that the plaintiffs were felling earth and raising dwellings on the suit land shows that defendant No. 1 and 2 are living in the same address of Dinanath Sen Road. Case of defendant No.1 on knowledge is that on 8-8-1995 he came to know from Zinnah and others for the first time about the existence of the deed exhibit No. 4 and then, he obtained the deeds of the suit land. So, he came to know about all subsequent transfers and the appearance of the plaintiffs on the suit land. But he did neither make the plaintiffs parties in his suit nor did he challenge the subsequent transactions. In the present suit, why Parol Bala who is living with him did not contest the suit nor was she examined has not been explained. Moreover, defendant No. 1 failed to adduce an iota of documents to show his presence and enjoyment of the suit land over the period from May, 1969 to 1995. To prove his claim that he was still a citizen of Bangladesh, defendant No.1 produced a passport issued at Dhaka on 11-2-1998 giving permanent address as Bangladesh. Trial Court was of the view that such a passport could be easily obtained in Bangladesh. The defendant No. 1 could adduce no other evidence oral or documentary. Above facts and circumstances as found by the trial Court are sufficient to justify its conclusion but did not find any consideration-in the judgment of the Court of appeal below.

18. For decision in the appeal, the appellate Court just relied upon the opinion of the handwriting expert in the earlier suit and the findings in the judgment on title and possession to justify its conclusion forgetting the fact that the very judgment has been impugned in this suit. When, a judgment and decree are impeached in a subsequent suit as collusive and fraudulent, the Court is required to consider the facts and circumstances upon which subsequent suit is based, and transpired at the trial. Findings of such impugned judgment cannot given any answer to the issues of collusion or fraud in the subsequent suit.

19. The appellate Court appears to have given its all considerations on the title and possession as if it was a suit for declaration of title and possession. It excluded the title deeds of the plaintiffs on the ground that the plaintiffs failed to examine neither the scribe nor the executant of their deeds. But record shows that Sahabuddin who sold the lands to the plaintiffs came before the Court and on oath admitted as PW 4 that he transferred the suit land to the plaintiffs by those sale deeds exhibit 9 series and delivered possession. It rejected the oral evidence of the plaintiffs without considering their entire evidence. It also failed to notice the fact that the plaintiffs have come from various parts of Bangladesh and on different dates purchased the land for the purpose of residence. One of them is not supposed to know every detail of the facts in respect of others. Besides, the notice dated 8-7-1998 issued by the Demra Police, the report of the Advocate Commissioner is the most important evidence on record on possession. When the defendant No.1 claimed the suit land as agricultural land, an Advocate Commissioner was appointed to ascertain the present position and nature of the suit land, namely, whether there is any paddy in the land and also the-number of structures standing thereon. After investigation, the Advocate Commissioner submitted his report on 11-5-1999 with a sketch map. The report was accepted without any objection. Sketch map clearly shows that the entire suit land is divided into plots for residential purposes with a road leading through the middle' of the land for access. Major portion of the land is occupied by different huts. Advocate Commissioner found 8 CI Sheet sheds, 6 semi-pucca and two pucca residential quarters. He definitely reported that he did not find any paddy field. This report together with the sketch map exhibit No.6 belies the case of defendant No.1 that the suit land is a nal land and his borgadar DW-1 cultivates the land with tractor. But such evidence was totally excluded by the appellate Court from consideration on the ground that why the Advocate Commissioner could not say the area of the land or the boundary thereof. The appellate Court failed to notice that such statements were made to questions asked beyond the terms of the reference for investigation, and he had to reply from his memory. Other PWs in chorus stated that the plaintiffs possess the suit land. Against the voluminous documentary evidence of the plaintiffs including rent receipts and RS khatian over a period of about 30 years, the defendant has got not an iota of evidence. But the Court of appeal below found that the plaintiffs do not know the suit land.

20. Curiously, the appellate Court has discovered that many of the plaintiffs did not sign the plaint. But we find that 16 out of 18 plaintiffs signed the plaint and the attorney signed on behalf of other two plaintiffs. In the nature of the suit, this is absolutely unnecessary exercise.

21. In the circumstances and on the evidence on record, the trial Court has correctly declared that the judgment and decree 24-5-1998 and 31-5-1998 respectively as obtained by defendant No. 1 in previous Title suit No. 51 of 1997 was obtained by collusion and practicing fraud in getting cancellation of the sale deed dated 14-5-1969, exhibit No.4. When such decree goes, whatever the cloud cast over the title of the plaintiffs is also cleared. It is also found that the findings of the Court of appeal below on title and possession and the decision in the appeal was arrived at on misreading and non-reading of the evidence on record and without application of any judicial mind. Such decision has no doubt resulted in serious miscarriage of justice. The judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below therefore cannot be sustained in law.

<u>22. Let me now consider the submission of Mr Garib Newaz that the suit is hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for failing of the plaintiffs to seek further declaration of title in the suit land. He also cites decisions in the case of MA Mallik vs NH Mallik, 1986 BCR (AD) 56 and that of Ishaque Mia and another vs Abdul Mazid and others, 48 DLR 465. According to him, the plaintiffs were further required to have prayed for declaration of title in the suit land. This issue was never raised before. Not even before the Court of appeal below. I shall however consider the question.</u>

In the case of MA Mallik, the Appellate Division has held.

"In view of the clear proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act there is no hesitation in saying that without prayer for consequential relief such suit should not be maintained."

23. The suit was brought for declaration that decree passed in Title Suit No. 69 of 1961 is fraudulent, void, collusive, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff. Leave granted to consider question whether the suit for declaration of title simpliciter could be maintained? Plaintiff was not a party to the suit. In coming to the above view, the Appellate Division did not elaborate what other relief ought to have been sought for. . Relying on the decision, a single bench in the case of Ishaque Mia held,

"Both the Courts below have held that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their title and possession and that in that circumstances it must be held that the plaintiffs were not entitled to a decree for simple declaration that the sale decree in Title Suit No. 561 of 1976 was obtained fraudulently, was illegal and not binding on him."

But in Moulavi Abdul Mannan vs Mohammed Rafiqul Islam, 46 DLR 493 another single bench held,

"when a decree adversely affects a person not a party to a decree he may file a suit for declaring the same not binding on him and get the same set aside if found illegal as in the present case."

The question was elaborately discussed by the Appellate Division 'in the case of Sufia Khanam Chowdhury vs Faizunnessa Chowdhury, 39 DLR (AD) 46, Appellate Division has held,

"If, by an instrument a person's right and title is clouded or threatened, he may seek a declaration under this section to the effect that by the instrument his right and title has not been affected or that any other person who denies his title or claims title in himself has not acquired any right or title. If the suit is for a declaration that a written instrument, whether it is a sale deed or a Court's decree, "is void", it clearly comes under section 39, since it is covered by the expression "any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable." But if a further prayer is included in the suit that by the void instrument the plaintiffs right has not been affected, then this prayer comes straight under section 42; similarly, if this prayer is framed in a different form, that is, the defendant acquired no right or interest thereby, it will make no difference, for this prayer is also covered by section 42. If this suit includes the reliefs that the instruments in question is void and his right has not been affected thereby and, or, the defendant acquired no right thereby, then the reliefs are covered by both sections 39 and 42. In such cases provisions of section 39 and 42 will overlap.

24. It appears that earlier decision was brought to the notice of the Appellate Division. Under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, no Court shall make any declaration of title where the plaintiff is able to seek 'further relief than mere declaration but omits to do so. It has now been settled by long line of decisions interpreting the phrase 'further relief that the 'further relief referred to in the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act must be a relief flowing directly and necessarily from the declaration sought and a relief appropriate to and necessarily consequent on, the right or title asserted.

Sometimes, it is called consequential relief and a relief is said to be consequential only when the relief of declaration is essential to the grant of that relief. No relief is consequential if it cannot be granted without declaration.

<u>25. In the suit before me, the plaintiffs impeached the decree passed in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 on ground of collusion and fraud on the assertion that they are owners in possession of the suit since 1969 and the defendants having no right, title or possession obtained the decree in collusion with each other after about 30 years of their sale. The trial Court has found their title and possession in the suit land and also held the judgment and decree of the earlier Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 collusive and fraudulent. Appellate Court as stated above most erroneously reversed those findings. In such suit, the plaintiffs are not required to seek any other relief as further relief to their main relief of declaration. Furthermore, with due respect, a relief for further declaration of title in the suit land as submitted does not seem to be a further relief within the meaning of the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Submission has therefore no substance.</u>

26. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. No order as to costs. Impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below are set aside and those of the trial Court are hereby restored.

Send down the records.

End.
